Sea-squirt Oikopleura dioica is a pelagic tunicate characterized by a rapid life cycle and extreme thermal sensitivity. The total trunk length at birth is remarkably small, measuring just 0.0115 cm [Lb = 0.0115 cm], a value that reflects the minimal maternal provisioning typical of the genus. At elevated temperatures of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], hatching occurs after a very brief incubation period of approximately 0.33 days [ab = approximately 0.33 days], indicating that embryogenesis proceeds at a pace matched to the warm, oligotrophic waters the species inhabits. Newly hatched individuals weigh a mere 0.4 mug  in dry weight, highlighting the extreme economy of body construction at the onset of free-swimming life. This combination of minute neonatal dimensions and a condensed embryonic phase is a common adaptive strategy among small-bodied appendicularians that must exploit ephemeral phytoplankton blooms.

Under laboratory conditions maintained at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], growing juveniles of Oikopleura dioica exhibit a striking increase in body mass over the first week of development. By day eight, the average dry weight of an individual reaches 52.6 mug , which represents more than a hundredfold increase from the birth weight at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. Concurrently, the total trunk length attains 0.1226 cm , a dimension that is easily visible under a dissecting microscope at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. These elevated growth rates are possible because the animal invests heavily in a large, gelatinous house that functions as both a filtration apparatus and a physical barrier against small predators. The house is periodically shed and replaced, an energetically costly process that nonetheless enables efficient collection of picoplankton and thus fuels the rapid biomass accumulation observed.

The species shows a pronounced thermal modulation of its demographic characteristics, with cooler conditions extending the reproductive window. When reared at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], individual Oikopleura dioica attain a maximum lifespan of 8.0 d [am = 8.0 d], which is considerably longer than the lifespan recorded at warmer temperatures. This extension of the survival period is accompanied by a corresponding increase in lifetime fecundity. Under the same thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females produce a total of 164.63 eggs at death , a substantial output for a micrometazoan of this body size. The ability to modulate both longevity and cumulative egg production as a function of ambient temperature suggests a flexible life-history strategy that can be tuned to local oceanographic conditions.

The reproductive biology of Oikopleura dioica is closely tied to its short lifespan. Gravid females are observed to release their eggs directly into the water column upon completion of the adult stage, a semelparous mode that maximizes the number of gametes shed in a single terminal spawning event. The total egg output at death of 164.63 eggs at death  at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] is a remarkably high number for an organism weighing only a few tens of micrograms. This fecundity is achieved through the simultaneous maturation of numerous oocytes within the ovary during the final days of life. Once released, the eggs are fertilized externally, and the resulting embryos develop rapidly, with the embryonic period at 22 °C being only 0.33 d [ab = 0.33 d], as measured in controlled temperature studies at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C].

Comparative analyses within the class Appendicularia reveal that Oikopleura dioica exhibits one of the most condensed life cycles known among marine zooplankton. The trunk length increase from 0.0115 cm [Lb = 0.0115 cm] at birth to 0.1226 cm  by day eight at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] represents a tenfold linear gain in only a week. Similarly, the dry weight escalates from 0.4 mug  to 52.6 mug  over the same interval at that temperature at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This pattern of rapid somatic growth is coupled with a life span that, at 8.0 d [am = 8.0 d] when maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], is among the shortest for any free-living metazoan. The extreme demographic pace of this species likely represents an adaptation to exploit short-lived patches of high food concentration in the upper ocean, a niche where speed of development directly translates into reproductive success.
